Let $M\in D^-(\mathcal A)$ and $N\in D^+(\mathcal A)$, with termwise bounded representatives. With supplied bounded-above projective models under [[thm-projective-complexes-model-the-bounded-above-derived-category]], define $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)=Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,N)$. Alternatively, with supplied bounded-below injective models under [[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]], use $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,I_N)$. The target is $D^+(\mathbf{Ab})$.

Here the cochain form of [[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]] has degree-$r$ term $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(M^i,N^{i+r})$ and differential $du=d_Nu-(-1)^ru d_M$. If $M^i=0$ above $b$ and $N^j=0$ below $a$, nonzero factors require $a-r\leq i\leq b$, a finite interval, and the whole term is zero for $r<a-b$.

This construction is a bifunctor on the declared derived categories. Indeed homotopies in either variable induce Hom-complex homotopies. Replacing a projective model by a homotopy equivalent one therefore changes its Hom complex by a homotopy equivalence. A quasi-isomorphism in the target has acyclic cone, whose Hom from $P_M$ is acyclic by K-projectivity; hence the Hom map is a quasi-isomorphism. This also follows degree by degree from [[prop-morphisms-from-a-homotopically-projective-complex-need-no-roof]], which identifies each Hom-complex cohomology with the corresponding derived Hom. The injective argument uses [[prop-morphisms-into-a-homotopically-injective-complex-need-no-roof]] and reverses the roles of source and target. Thus both variables descend through localization. When both systems exist, the quasi-isomorphisms $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,N)\to\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,I_N)\leftarrow\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,I_N)$ give their natural identification. Either one-sided resolution hypothesis suffices.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$**
is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms
$$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$
such that
$$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$
for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

This page uses the reindexing convention that a cochain complex $C^\bullet$ may
also be read as the chain complex with $(C^\sharp)_n:=C^{-n}$ and
$d^\sharp_n:=d^{-n}$, so that lower and upper indices differ only by the sign
of the grading.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category. Put

$$D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)[\mathrm{qis}^{-1}],\qquad Q:K(\mathcal A)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A).$$

Likewise $D^-,D^+,D^b$ initially mean the localizations of the termwise bounded variants of [[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]. Roof morphisms exist by [[lem-quasi-isomorphisms-admit-the-roof-calculus-in-the-homotopy-category]] and [[thm-the-calculus-of-fractions-constructs-the-localization]] under its standing size hypothesis: a small category of complexes, or supplied small cofinal denominator families. Every assertion of Hom sets is under that hypothesis. In the bounded module models, supplied replacements will separately exhibit those Hom sets. No general local-smallness theorem for unbounded $D(\mathcal A)$ is asserted.

The cone convention is $\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=Y^n\oplus X^{n+1}$, $d(y,x)=(d_Yy+fx,-d_Xx)$, and its triangle ends in $X[1]$.

derivations.claim: Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms of diagrams of $k$-vector spaces are formed objectwise, so a morphism of diagrams is an epimorphism exactly when it is surjective at every object, and a complex of diagrams is exact exactly when it is exact at every object. In particular exactness questions about $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ reduce to the vector spaces $N(p)$, and no diagram-level machinery beyond the objectwise one is used below.

For $p\in P$ define the diagram $Q_p$ by $Q_p(q)=k$ for $p\le q$ and $Q_p(q)=0$ otherwise, with the identity as structure map whenever both values are nonzero. A natural transformation $\varphi:Q_p\to N$ is determined by $\varphi_p(1)\in N(p)$, since for $q\ge p$ the component $\varphi_q$ must equal $N(p\to q)\circ\varphi_p$ and for $q\ngeq p$ the source $Q_p(q)$ is zero; conversely every vector $v\in N(p)$ extends by these formulas. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p,N)\cong N(p)$ by evaluation at $p$. Pulling back along the identification, a surjection $\pi:N\to N'$ induces the surjection $N(p)\to N'(p)$ by step 1.1, so every map $Q_p\to N'$ lifts to $N$ and $Q_p$ is projective. For a finite-dimensional $V$, a natural transformation $Q_p\otimes_kV\to N$ is likewise determined by its value at $p$, a $k$-linear map $V\to N(p)$, and conversely every such map extends uniquely by the structure maps of $N$, so $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p\otimes_kV,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,N(p))$; since $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,-)$ carries surjections to surjections — lift the images of a finite basis and extend linearly — the diagram $Q_p\otimes_kV$ is projective as well. A finite direct sum of projectives is projective, because $\operatorname{Hom}(\bigoplus_tX_t,N)\cong\prod_t\operatorname{Hom}(X_t,N)$ and a finite product of surjections of vector spaces is surjective by induction on the number of factors. Only finitely many basis vectors and summands occur at each step, so no choice principle is used.

For a diagram $N$ put $\mathcal B_n(N)=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}Q_{p_n}\otimes_kN(p_0)$ for $n\ge0$, with the face maps $\partial_i:\mathcal B_n(N)\to\mathcal B_{n-1}(N)$ ($0\le i\le n$) given on the summand of the chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n$ by: for $i=0$ apply the structure map $N(p_0)\to N(p_1)$ and delete $p_0$; for $0<i<n$ delete the inner vertex $p_i$, keeping the coefficient in $N(p_0)$ and the representable index $p_n$; for $i=n$ delete $p_n$ and use the natural map $Q_{p_n}\to Q_{p_{n-1}}$ (which is the identity on values) while keeping the coefficient. Let $\partial=\sum_i(-1)^i\partial_i$. The simplicial identities $\partial_i\partial_j=\partial_{j-1}\partial_i$ for $i<j$ hold because diagram transport $p\mapsto N(p)$ is functorial and the maps between representables compose, so $\partial^2=0$; this is a sign-alternating sum of a simplicial identity. Since chains of $P$ have at most $h$ strict inequalities, $\mathcal B_n(N)=0$ for $n>h$. Augment by the structure maps $\epsilon:\mathcal B_0(N)\to N$, $Q_p\otimes_kN(p)\to N$, which are natural.

Evaluate the augmented complex at $q\in P$. Its degree-$n$ part consists of the chains $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ with a vector of $N(p_0)$, the faces delete a vertex as in step 3.1, the last face being free to delete $q$, and the augmentation sends a length-zero chain $(p_0)$ to $N(p_0\to q)v$. Define a degree-$(-1)$-to-$0$ map $s_{-1}:N(q)\to\mathcal B_0(N)(q)$ by $v\mapsto(q,v)$, and for $n\ge0$ a degree-$n$-to-$n+1$ map $s_n$ on the summand of the chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ by $s_n(v)=(-1)^{n+1}(p_0<\cdots<p_n<q,\,v)$ when $p_n<q$, and $s_n=0$ when $p_n=q$. One checks $\partial s_n+s_{n-1}\partial=\mathrm{id}$ on each evaluated component: the appended simplex contributes through its last face with sign $(-1)^{n+1}\cdot(-1)^{n+1}=1$, every other face is matched by the corresponding appended term in $s\partial$ with opposite sign, and in degree zero the augmentation section cancels exactly the last-face term; when $p_n=q$ no simplex can be appended and $s\partial$ is the identity through $s_{-1}\epsilon$. Moreover $\epsilon$ is surjective on the evaluated complexes because $(q,v)\mapsto v$, so the augmented evaluated complex is exact in every degree. Exactness is objectwise by step 1.1, so $\epsilon:\mathcal B(N)\to N$ is a quasi-isomorphism; and if every $N(p)$ is finite-dimensional then every $\mathcal B_n(N)$ is a finite direct sum of projectives by step 2.1, so $\mathcal B(N)$ is a bounded projective resolution of $N$.

Let $A$ be a bounded complex of diagrams with finite-dimensional values, vanishing outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, with internal differentials $d_A$. Apply the bar construction of step 4.1 to each internal degree $u$, so $\mathcal B_n(A^u)$ has bar degree $n\in[0,h]$ and carries the internal differential $d_A:\mathcal B_n(A^u)\to\mathcal B_n(A^{u+1})$. The face maps $\partial$ commute with the maps induced by $d_A$, since they are built from the structure maps of the diagrams and from the fixed maps between representables. Take the total complex $\operatorname{Tot}$ with $\operatorname{Tot}^m=\bigoplus_{u-n=m}\mathcal B_n(A^u)$ and differential $D=d_A+(-1)^u\partial$ on the summand $\mathcal B_n(A^u)$; the sign $(-1)^u$ makes the horizontal and vertical parts anticommute, so $D^2=0$. Each column $u$ maps quasi-isomorphically to $A^u$ by step 4.1, so the rows of the mapping cone of $\operatorname{Tot}\to A$ are the mapping cones of the augmentations $\mathcal B(A^u)\to A^u$ and are acyclic; a bounded double complex with acyclic rows has acyclic total complex, by filtering by the finitely many internal degrees and inducting on the number of rows with the long exact homology sequence of the quotient by the top row. Hence $\operatorname{Tot}\to A$ is a quasi-isomorphism, $\operatorname{Tot}$ is a complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams by steps 2.1 and 4.1, and its total degrees $u-n$ lie in $[a-h,b]$.

Resolve the constant diagram $\underline k$ by its bar complex $\mathcal B(\underline k)$, a bounded complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams of the form of step 4.1 with $\underline k$ in internal degree $0$. Then $\mathbf R\lim M=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ is computed by the Hom complex $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal B(\underline k),M)$ of [F1], whose degree-$r$ term is $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal B(\underline k)^i,M^{i+r})$. Here $\mathcal B(\underline k)^{-n}=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}k$ is nonzero only for $0\le n\le h$ and $M^j=0$ for $j\notin[a,b]$, so by the vanishing rule of [F1] nonzero factors require $a-r\le i\le b$ with $-h\le i\le0$, that is $r\in[a,b+h]$. Concretely the bar-degree-$n$ part is the finite product $\prod_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}M(p_n)$, so every term is a finite product of finite-dimensional spaces, hence finite-dimensional. Thus $\mathbf R\lim M$ has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$.

For the pair $A,B$ concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$, resolve the source by the total bar model $P_A:=\operatorname{Tot}$ of step 5.1, concentrated in $[a-h,b]$, and apply [F1]: $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$ is computed by $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_A,B)$, whose degree-$r$ term is the finite product $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(P_A^i,B^{i+r})$. A nonzero factor requires $P_A^i
e0$ and $B^{i+r}
e0$, hence $a-h\le i\le b$ and $c\le i+r\le d$; so for $r<c-b$ every $i$ with $P_A^i
e0$ has $i+r<b+r<c$ and for $r>d-a+h$ every such $i$ has $i+r>d$, and in both cases every factor of the term vanishes. Thus the model is concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. Each $\operatorname{Hom}(P_A^i,B^{i+r})$ is a space of linear maps between finite-dimensional spaces and only finitely many $i$ occur in each degree, so every term is finite-dimensional.

Let $K/k$ be a field extension, and write the base-changed inputs as $K\otimes_kM$, $K\otimes_kA$, $K\otimes_kB$, diagrams over $K$. The models built in steps 5.2 and 6.1 have terms obtained from the values $M(p)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A(p),B(q))$ by finite sums, finite products and the fixed face and structure maps; extending scalars commutes with finite direct sums, with finite products and, between finite-dimensional spaces, with Hom spaces, so $K\otimes_k$ of the model for $(M,A,B)$ is the model for the base-changed inputs, with the same signs and differentials. Tensoring with $K$ preserves kernels and images of linear maps between finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and hence commutes with the homology of a bounded complex of such spaces, so the cohomology of the base-changed model is the base change of the cohomology of the original model. This proves both base-change assertions. For the empty poset there are no chains, the diagram sections and the Hom complex vanish by the same product formulas, and the asserted model is zero.

boundaries.evidence: The empty poset is covered by the stated convention and by step 7.1: there are no chains, the product formulas vanish, and the diagram sections and the derived Hom model are zero.

boundaries.reason: The field is arbitrary and no denominator or zero divisor occurs; zero coefficients and the zero diagram are handled by the empty-sum conventions of the bar construction.
A one-element poset is not singled out; the bounds hold uniformly, with bar length zero when there are no strict inequalities.
There is no degenerate parameter; every finite poset is treated uniformly by the bar construction of step 3.1.

boundaries.evidence: The degree endpoints are exactly the content of the bounds: step 5.2 and step 6.1 verify the stated concentration ranges, including the extremal degrees obtained from the longest chain.
Only finite direct sums, finite products and Hom spaces of finite-dimensional spaces occur, as recorded in step 2.1 and step 7.1; nothing is selected and the item's axiom use is none.

boundaries.reason: The phrase 'exactly when' in the statement defines the arrows of the poset category; the model bounds themselves are asserted one way and no theorem biconditional is proved.
No converse is claimed: the models are not asserted to be the unique finite-dimensional models, only that these exist with the stated bounds.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every metric space is paracompact.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $p, q \in X$ with
$p \ne q$. Put $r := d(p,q)/2$. Then $r > 0$ and

$$B(p,r) \cap B(q,r) = \emptyset .$$

Both sets are open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]) and contain $p$
respectively $q$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), so every metric space is **Hausdorff**:
distinct points are separated by disjoint open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $X$ is paracompact and Hausdorff and
$\mathcal U$ is an open cover, there are a set $S$, a map $s\mapsto U_s$ from
$S$ into $\mathcal U$, and locally finite open covers $\{V_s\}_{s\in S}$ and
$\{W_s\}_{s\in S}$ with
$$\overline{V_s}\subseteq W_s\subseteq\overline{W_s}\subseteq U_s\quad(s\in S).$$

The inclusion $C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(X;G)\hookrightarrow C_\bullet(X;G)$
induces an isomorphism on homology.

Let $H:X\times I\to Y$ be a homotopy from $f$ to $g$. Then the prism operator
$P_H$ of [[def-prism-operator-for-a-homotopy]] satisfies
$$g_\#-f_\#=\partial P_H+P_H\partial$$
as homomorphisms $C_n(X;G)\to C_n(Y;G)$ for every $n\geq 1$ and every abelian
group $G$. In degree $0$, the same identity reduces to
$$g_{\#,0}-f_{\#,0}=\partial P_H:C_0(X;G)\to C_0(Y;G).$$

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. For every $x\in X$,
the sheafification map induces a bijection
$$\eta_{\mathcal F,x}:\mathcal F_x\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }(a\mathcal F)_x.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a topological space and let
$$0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }\mathcal H\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on $X$
([[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]]) in which $\mathcal F$ is flasque
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]).

1. For every open subset $U\subseteq X$ the map
   $\varphi_U:\mathcal G(U)\to\mathcal H(U)$ is surjective.
2. If moreover $\mathcal G$ is flasque, then $\mathcal H$ is flasque.

The Axiom of Choice is used exactly once, to apply Zorn's lemma in part 1
([[thm-zorn]], [[cor-ac-iff-zorn]]).

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian
groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]). For open subsets
$U\subseteq V\subseteq X$ write
$$\rho^V_U:\mathcal F(V)\longrightarrow\mathcal F(U)$$
for the restriction map of $\mathcal F$
([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]).

Then $\mathcal F$ is **flasque**, also called **flabby**, when each of these
restriction maps is surjective: for all open $U\subseteq V\subseteq X$ the map
$\rho^V_U$ is onto. Equivalently, $\mathcal F$ is flasque when every section of
$\mathcal F$ over an open subset $U$ extends to every larger open subset $V$,
that is, when for every $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ there is $t\in\mathcal F(V)$ with
$t|_U=s$.

The same condition on restriction maps defines flasque sheaves of sets and
flasque sheaves of modules over a sheaf of rings; on this page the notion is
used for sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $U$.

For an open set $V \subseteq X$, define
$$(j_!\mathcal F)(V) := \left\{ s\in \mathcal F(V\cap U): \operatorname{Supp}(s)\text{ is closed in }V \right\}.$$
Equivalently, $s$ lies in $(j_!\mathcal F)(V)$ exactly when for every
$x\in V\setminus U$ there exists an open neighbourhood $W_x \subseteq V$ with
$$
s|_{W_x\cap U}=0.
$$

Restriction maps are inherited from $\mathcal F$, so $j_!\mathcal F$ is a
subsheaf of $j_*\mathcal F$. When $V \subseteq U$, the support condition is
vacuous and
$$
(j_!\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V).
$$

This is the **extension by zero** of $\mathcal F$ along $j$. It is distinct in
general from the ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: (Flasque $k$-sheaves are acyclic.) Let $\mathcal I$ be an injective $k$-sheaf. For opens $U\subseteq V$ the canonical extension-by-zero map $j_{U!}k_U\to j_{V!}k_V$ is a monomorphism of $k$-sheaves: a section of $j_{U!}k_U$ over an open $W$ is a locally constant function on $W\cap U$ whose support is closed in $W$, and as a section of $k_X$ over $W$ it is supported in $U\subseteq V$, hence lies in $j_{V!}k_V(W)$. By [F10] the adjunction identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_{U!}k_U,\mathcal I)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_U(k_U,\mathcal I|_U)\cong\mathcal I(U)$, and likewise with $V$ in place of $U$. Injectivity of $\mathcal I$ therefore makes the restriction $\mathcal I(V)\to\mathcal I(U)$ surjective, so $\mathcal I$ is flasque by [F9]. Now let $F$ be a flasque $k$-sheaf and embed it into an injective $\mathcal I$ using [F7], with quotient $Q$. The underlying sequence of abelian sheaves has flasque kernel $F$, so by [F8] every section of $Q$ lifts over every open set and $Q$ is flasque. Writing $H^q(U,-)$ for the derived functors of the $k$-linear sections functor at $U$ as in [F7], the long exact sequence gives $H^1(U,F)=0$ and $H^{n+1}(U,F)\cong H^n(U,Q)$ for $n\ge1$; since $Q$ is again flasque this proves $H^n(U,F)=0$ for all $n\ge1$ by induction on $n$, uniformly over all flasque $k$-sheaves. Only underlying section lifting uses [F8]; no assertion that a $k$-injective is an injective abelian sheaf is made.

(Flasque singular-cochain sheaves.) Let $C^n(U;k)$ be the $k$-vector space of functions on the singular $n$-simplices of $X$ with image in $U$, with the usual cochain differential, and let $\mathcal C^n$ be its sheafification. Represent a section $s\in\mathcal C^n(U)$ by cochains $c_i$ on an open cover $\{U_i\}$ of $U$: this is what a section of the sheafification is, by [F6]. Since $X$ is metric it is paracompact by [F1] and Hausdorff by [F2], so [F3] applied to the cover $\{U_i\}$ yields a locally finite open cover $\{W_i\}_{i\in I}$ refining it, with each $W_i$ contained in some member $U_{j(i)}$. Choose such an index $j(i)$ for each $i$ and write $c_i$ for $c_{j(i)}$; these are choices, covered by [A1]. Define a cochain $c$ on $X$ by assigning to a singular simplex $\sigma$ whose image lies in some $W_i$ the value $c_i(\sigma)$, and the value $0$ if the image lies in no $W_i$. This defines a function on the set of singular simplices, hence a cochain. Once the verification carried out below is granted, $C^n(V;k)\to\mathcal C^n(V)$ is surjective for every open $V$, because the construction produces a global representative for every section over $V$, and then a section over $U$ extends to one over any larger $V$; surjectivity of these maps says exactly that the restriction maps $\mathcal C^n(V)\to\mathcal C^n(U)$ are surjective. Hence each $\mathcal C^n$ is flasque by [F9].

(The assignment gives the prescribed germs.) Fix $x\in U$. Since $\{W_i\}$ is locally finite the set $J_x=\{i:x\in\overline{W_i}\}$ is finite, and there is an open neighbourhood of $x$ meeting none of the sets $W_i$ with $i\notin J_x$. The cochains $c_i$ for $i\in J_x$ represent the same section $s$ on the intersections of their domains with a neighbourhood of $x$; their classes in the presheaf stalk $\mathcal C^n_x$ therefore have a common image in the sheaf stalk, and since sheafification induces a bijection on stalks by [F6], the classes of the $c_i$ in the presheaf stalk are equal. Equality in the stalk of the presheaf means that the finitely many cochains $c_i$, $i\in J_x$, agree as presheaf cochains on one common neighbourhood $N$ of $x$: the stalk is the filtered colimit of the section sets over the neighbourhoods, and intersections make the index system directed. Shrink $N$ so that it is contained in some $W_{i_0}$ and meets no $W_i$ with $i\notin J_x$. A singular simplex with image entirely in $N$ is then contained in some $W_i$, necessarily with $i\in J_x$, and the value $c_i(\sigma)$ assigned to it equals $c_{i_0}(\sigma)$ for every admissible $i$ by the agreement on $N$; hence the value assigned by the cochain $c$ of step 1.2 is independent of the admissible index and equals the value of $c_{i_0}$, which represents $s$ near $x$. Thus $c$ represents $s$ in every germ, and the surjectivity and flasqueness claims of step 1.2 hold.

(The augmented complex is a flasque resolution.) The augmentation $k_X\to\mathcal C^0$ sends the locally constant function $1$ to the zero-cochain that is constant one on points. By [F6] the stalk of each $\mathcal C^n$ at $x$ is the filtered colimit, over the open neighbourhoods $V$ of $x$, of the cochain complexes $C^*(V;k)$, and filtered colimits of $k$-vector spaces preserve exactness, so the cohomology of the stalk complex is the colimit of the cohomology of these complexes. By hypothesis the contractible open neighbourhoods of $x$ are cofinal; a contraction of such a $V$ together with [F5] gives that the identity of $V$ and a constant map to a point induce the same map on cohomology, so $H^0_{\operatorname{sing}}(V;k)\cong k$ and $H^n_{\operatorname{sing}}(V;k)=0$ for $n\ge1$, the point's cochain complex being $k$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees. Every cohomology class on a neighbourhood is therefore represented on a contractible one and is either constant or dies, so the stalk complex is exact in positive degrees with kernel $k$ in degree zero, the kernel being the constant functions. Hence $k_X\to\mathcal C^0\to\mathcal C^1\to\cdots$ is a flasque resolution of $k_X$, and by step 1.1 its sections compute the derived cohomology of $k_X$; the derived groups are those formed with the $k$-linear injective resolutions of [F7].

(Identification with singular cohomology.) The map $C^*(X;k)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)$ given by the global construction of step 1.2 is surjective by step 2.1. Let $N^*$ be its kernel. A cochain lies in $N^*$ exactly when it vanishes on all simplices contained in some member of some open cover of $X$: a cochain has zero germ at $x$ exactly when it vanishes on all simplices of some neighbourhood of $x$ by [F6], and a cochain vanishing on the small simplices of a cover has zero germ everywhere, while conversely the neighbourhoods of all points form such a cover. For an open cover $\mathcal U$ let $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ be the subcomplex of cochains vanishing on the $\mathcal U$-small singular chains. By [F4] applied with coefficients in the field $k$, the inclusion of the small chain complex into all chains is a homology isomorphism, so the quotient chain complex is acyclic; over a field an acyclic chain complex of possibly infinite-dimensional spaces splits degreewise into its boundaries and a complementary subspace, and dualizing such a splitting shows that the Hom of the quotient into $k$ is acyclic. Since restriction of functions to the subcomplex of small chains is surjective, this dual complex is exactly $K^*_{\mathcal U}$; hence $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ is acyclic. The complexes $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ are directed by refinement, and their union is $N^*$. A cocycle in the union lies in one $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ and is a coboundary there, so $N^*$ is acyclic. The long exact sequence of the short exact sequence of cochain complexes $0\to N^*\to C^*(X;k)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)\to0$ therefore identifies $H^*_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$ with the cohomology of $\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)$.

Conclusion for $X$. Step 3.1 and step 3.2 identify the derived cohomology of $k_X$ with $H^*_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$, and the identifications come from restriction and sheafification, so they are natural in $X$; this is the asserted isomorphism, in the conventions for derived sheaf cohomology fixed by [F7] and compared with the abelian-sheaf definition of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]].

Open subspaces and the stated consequences. Every open subspace $Y\subseteq X$ is again metric and has the inherited contractible-open basis, and every step above is local: the construction of $\mathcal C^n$ restricts, the flasqueness argument applies to $Y$ in place of $X$, and the splitting argument of step 3.2 applies to the restricted covers. Hence the isomorphism also holds on every open subset. If $X$ is nonempty and contractible, then by [F5] its singular cohomology is that of a point, namely $k$ in degree zero and zero otherwise, and the identification gives the same for $H^*(X,k_X)$. For a finite-polyhedral realization, a point of a simplex $\sigma$ has arbitrarily small contractible open neighbourhoods obtained by requiring its $\sigma$-coordinates to stay close to their positive values and its other coordinates to have sufficiently small sum; an open star, or the nonempty intersection of an open star with a closed simplex, is a convex, hence linearly contractible, subset of the realization and inherits a basis of such neighbourhoods in its subspace topology. The comparison and the acyclicity conclusion therefore apply to exactly these neighbourhoods, and no triangulation equivalence of derived categories is used.

boundaries.evidence: For the empty space both sides vanish in every degree, since the constant sheaf has zero global sections and the singular cochain complex is zero, so the statement holds as the zero isomorphism.
The degree-zero computation is carried out in step 5.1 for the nonempty contractible case, where the common value is the field k; no zero value of a parameter is assumed anywhere.
The one-point space satisfies the local hypothesis trivially, and the contractible-space clause of step 5.1 gives its constant-sheaf cohomology as the field k in degree zero and zero otherwise.

No interval endpoints or limiting boundary values occur; the degrees are arbitrary and the isomorphisms are stated in every degree.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

With supplied bounded-below injective replacements $j_X:X\to I_X$ (and DC or supplied homotopy extensions), $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories. For a bounded-below complex $I$, K-injectivity can be tested using only bounded-below acyclic inputs.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

A **triangulated subcategory** of $\mathcal T$ is a full additive subcategory
closed under $[1]$ and $[-1]$ such that, with the inherited distinguished
triangles, it satisfies the triangulated axioms. Equivalently in this full
setting it is closed under the two-out-of-three operation on distinguished
triangles.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$x\in X$. Then there is a canonical isomorphism
$$
(f^{-1}\mathcal G)_x\cong \mathcal G_{f(x)}.
$$

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category. Put

$$D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)[\mathrm{qis}^{-1}],\qquad Q:K(\mathcal A)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A).$$

Likewise $D^-,D^+,D^b$ initially mean the localizations of the termwise bounded variants of [[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]. Roof morphisms exist by [[lem-quasi-isomorphisms-admit-the-roof-calculus-in-the-homotopy-category]] and [[thm-the-calculus-of-fractions-constructs-the-localization]] under its standing size hypothesis: a small category of complexes, or supplied small cofinal denominator families. Every assertion of Hom sets is under that hypothesis. In the bounded module models, supplied replacements will separately exhibit those Hom sets. No general local-smallness theorem for unbounded $D(\mathcal A)$ is asserted.

The cone convention is $\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=Y^n\oplus X^{n+1}$, $d(y,x)=(d_Yy+fx,-d_Xx)$, and its triangle ends in $X[1]$.

Let $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ be a morphism of sheaves of abelian
groups on a topological space $X$.

The **kernel sheaf** is the subsheaf
$$
\ker(\varphi)\subseteq \mathcal F
$$
defined objectwise by
$$
\ker(\varphi)(U):=\ker\!\bigl(\varphi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\bigr).
$$

The **cokernel presheaf** is
$$
U\longmapsto \operatorname{coker}\!\bigl(\varphi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\bigr),
$$
and the **cokernel sheaf** $\operatorname{coker}(\varphi)$ is its
sheafification.

The **image presheaf** is
$$
U\longmapsto \operatorname{im}\!\bigl(\varphi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\bigr),
$$
and the **image sheaf** $\operatorname{im}(\varphi)$ is its sheafification.

For sheaves of modules on a ringed space, the same formulas are taken in the
corresponding module categories on each open set.

Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical
algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as
a topological space with its analytic topology
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and
let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is
an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its
bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the
conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the
standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large;
   and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth
   algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$
   ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such
   that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the
   restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank
   ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent
sheaves. We use the shift convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A
groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through
an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it
is quantified existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier
stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or
common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted by this definition.
Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness
and shifts a witnessing stratification nowhere, so the class is closed under
shifts and under isomorphisms in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$. No choice
principle is used.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an
affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem and no choice principle is asserted: nothing is
selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.

Let $S$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let $k$ be a field
and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $S$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]]). Then $\mathcal F$ is **locally
constant of finite rank** if every point $x\in S$ has an open neighbourhood
$U\subseteq S$ for which there are an integer $n\ge0$ and an isomorphism of
sheaves on $U$
$$\mathcal F|_U\;\cong\;k_U^{\,n},$$
where $k_U$ is the constant sheaf on $U$ with value $k$ and $\mathcal F|_U$ is
the restriction of $\mathcal F$ to the open subspace $U$
([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]], [[def-morphism-of-presheaves]],
[[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]). A sheaf with
this property is also called a **finite-rank local system of $k$-vector spaces**
on $S$. This is a property of the sheaf on the space; no identification of such
sheaves with functors on the fundamental groupoid is part of the definition.

The sheaf $k_U^{\,n}$ is the $n$-fold direct sum of $k_U$ in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, with $k_U^{\,0}$ the zero sheaf; its sections over
an open $W\subseteq U$ are the locally constant functions $W\to k^n$. The
integer $n$ is quantified locally, so no global rank is asserted and the rank
may differ from point to point; the definition asserts no existence of a global
trivialization. The final sentence records only that a functorial groupoid
presentation of local systems is a different, uncompared object here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: (Setup.) A sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $X$ is an $\mathcal O_X$-module for the ringed space $(X,k_X)$ and conversely, and the stalk $k$ is a local ring, so $(X,k_X)$ is a locally ringed space with $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)=\mathrm{Mod}(k_X)$; this category is abelian, and $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is taken with the cochain conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], every Hom-set assertion being under its standing smallness hypothesis. In the second part, $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded and $\mathfrak S$-constructible.

(Injective models.) By [F1] applied to $(X,k_X)$ every $k$-sheaf $\mathcal F$ receives one specific injective resolution $0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$, i.e. a supplied bounded-below injective replacement; these exist under AC, which is assumed. By [F3] AC supplies the dependent choice required by [F2], so $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories. Consequently Hom groups in $D^+$, and therefore Hom groups between bounded complexes, are computed by homotopy classes of maps between these specific injective replacements. This is exactly the model statement for $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$.

(Shifts and isomorphisms.) Fix the stratification $\mathfrak S$ and let $A\in D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$. For the shift, $H^n(A[m])=H^{n+m}(A)$ by [F7], so on each stratum the restriction of $H^n(A[m])$ is the shift of the restriction of $H^{n+m}(A)$, which is locally constant of finite rank by [F9] and [F10]; the cohomological support is merely reindexed, so $A[m]\in D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ for every $m$. If $A\cong A'$ in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ then the cohomology sheaves are isomorphic, because $H^j$ is additive on the homotopy category and quasi-isomorphisms induce isomorphisms on cohomology and are inverted in the localization; hence $A'\in D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ as well. Thus the subcategory is closed under shifts and contains every complex isomorphic to one of its objects.

(Cones on one stratum.) Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism of $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ with cone $C(f)$. Fix a stratum $S$ of $\mathfrak S$, a point $s\in S$ and an open neighbourhood $V$ of $s$ in $X$ such that $S\cap V$ is closed in $V$; sheaves on the locally closed subspace $S$ near $s$ are computed on such pieces. Restriction to a subspace has, at a point, the stalk over the image point by [F6], and exactness of sequences of sheaves can be tested on stalks by [F6]; since finite direct sums and shifts are computed stalkwise from the same data, restriction commutes with the finite direct sums, the shifts and the differentials appearing in the cone formula $\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=B^n\oplus A^{n+1}$ of [F7]. Hence $C(f)|_S$ is the cone of the induced chain map $f|_S:A|_S\to B|_S$, and the long exact cohomology sequence of the cone triangle [F4] gives, in every degree, a short exact sequence of sheaves on $S$ $0\to\operatorname{coker}(f^j)\to H^j(C(f))|_S\to\ker(f^{j+1})\to0$ where $f^j:H^j(A)|_S\to H^j(B)|_S$ is the map induced on cohomology sheaves. Here $H^j(A)|_S$ and $H^j(B)|_S$ are locally constant of finite rank by [F9] and [F10]. On a neighbourhood where both trivialize, $f^j$ becomes a matrix whose entries are locally constant functions; shrinking to a connected neighbourhood makes every entry constant, and then the kernel, image and cokernel of a linear map are the constant sheaves with the corresponding kernel, image and cokernel as values, these being computed objectwise and sheafified in agreement with [F8]. Hence $\ker(f^{j+1})$ and $\operatorname{coker}(f^j)$ are locally constant of finite rank on $S$.

(Extensions of local systems are local systems.) Let $0\to K\to E\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }Q\to0$ be a short exact sequence of $k$-sheaves on a space $Y$ in which $K$ and $Q$ are locally constant of finite rank. Fix $y\in Y$ and a neighbourhood on which $K$ and $Q$ trivialize; shrink it to a connected neighbourhood $N$ over which $Q$ has a finite basis of constant sections $e_1,\dots,e_q$. The stalk map $\pi_y:E_y\to Q_y$ is surjective, so the finitely many basis germs lift to elements of $E_y$; each lift is represented by a section over some neighbourhood of $y$, and on a common smaller neighbourhood $N'\subseteq N$ the images of these sections are the constant sections $e_1,\dots,e_q$, by the stalkwise description of sheaf maps. Define $s:Q|_{N'}\to E|_{N'}$ on sections over an open $W\subseteq N'$ by sending the section $\sum_ia_ie_i|_W$, with locally constant functions $a_i:W\to k$, to the section $\sum_ia_it_i|_W$, where $t_i$ are the lifted sections; this is well defined, compatible with restrictions, $k$-linear on sections, and satisfies $\pi\circ s=\operatorname{id}$. Then $(u,v)\mapsto u+s(v)$ is a morphism $K|_{N'}\oplus Q|_{N'}\to E|_{N'}$ which is injective on every stalk, since $\pi(u+s(v))=v$ vanishes only for $v=0$ and then $u=0$; the stalk exact sequence $0\to K_y\to E_y\to Q_y\to0$ of vector spaces has $\dim E_y=\dim K_y+\dim Q_y$ and the vector-space sequence splits, so the injective stalk maps are isomorphisms. A morphism of sheaves that is an isomorphism on every stalk is an isomorphism, so $E|_{N'}\cong K|_{N'}\oplus Q|_{N'}$ is a direct sum of sheaves locally constant of finite rank, hence itself locally constant of finite rank. No choice beyond finitely many lifts and the local trivializations is used.

(Cone constructibility.) Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical
algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as
a topological space with its analytic topology
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and
let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is
an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its
bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the
conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the
standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large;
   and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth
   algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$
   ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such
   that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the
   restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank
   ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent
sheaves. We use the shift convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A
groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through
an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it
is quantified existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier
stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or
common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted by this definition.
Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness
and shifts a witnessing stratification nowhere, so the class is closed under
shifts and under isomorphisms in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$. No choice
principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological
space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space
$(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$
([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally
small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and
iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific
injective resolution
([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). These resolutions are
bounded-below injective replacements, so with the dependent choice supplied by
AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below
injective complexes model the bounded derived category:
$K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to
D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence, and morphisms of the bounded
derived category are computed by these replacements
([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let
$\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier
condition of $X$
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded
and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$
([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under
shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded
algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one
common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is
bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace
([[def-topological-space]]) with closed complement $Z=X\setminus U$, let
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of the subspace
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups
on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]).
Write $\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F|_Z:=i^{-1}\mathcal F$ for
the restrictions ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]). Then:

1. the adjoint transpose of the identity of $\mathcal F|_U$ under the adjunction
   of [[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]] and the unit of the
   adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) fit into a short exact
   sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$
   $$0\to j_!(\mathcal F|_U)\to\mathcal F\to i_*(\mathcal F|_Z)\to0,$$
   where $j_!$ is extension by zero ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]]) and
   $i_*$ is the direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]],
   [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]); exactness is that of
   [[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]];
2. if $\mathcal F=\mathbb Z_X$ is the constant sheaf with value $\mathbb Z$ on
   $X$, then $\mathcal F|_U$ is canonically isomorphic to the constant sheaf
   $\mathbb Z_U$ on $U$, so the sequence of clause 1 reads
   $0\to j_!(\mathbb Z_U)\to\mathbb Z_X\to i_*(\mathcal F|_Z)\to0$ up to that
   canonical isomorphism.

Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of a closed subset
$Z\subseteq X$ carrying the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and
let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]])
whose stalks vanish off $Z$, that is $\mathcal G_x=0$ for every $x\in X\setminus Z$
([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]). Then the unit
$$\eta:\mathcal G\longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}\mathcal G$$
of the adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) between inverse image
and direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]], [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]) is an
isomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups; equivalently
$\mathcal G\cong i_*(\mathcal G|_Z)$ under the identification
$\mathcal G|_Z=i^{-1}\mathcal G$ ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]).

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be a chain map in an additive category. The
**mapping cone** of $f$ is the chain complex $\operatorname{Cone}(f)_\bullet$
whose degree-$n$ term is
$$\operatorname{Cone}(f)_n:=D_n\oplus C[1]_n=D_n\oplus C_{n-1},$$
and whose differential is
$$d_n^{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}(y,x):=(d_n^D(y)+f_{n-1}(x),-d_{n-1}^C(x)).$$

Thus $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ is the direct sum of $D$ and the shift $C[1]$ as
a graded object, with the off-diagonal term given by $f$.

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: A sheaf on the one-point space is its vector space of global sections, so a bounded complex of $k$-sheaves on the point is a bounded complex of $k$-vector spaces, and the unique finite smooth stratification of the point makes constructibility with respect to it exactly the condition that every cohomology space be finite-dimensional by [F1]. A bounded complex whose cohomology is finite-dimensional is isomorphic in the derived category to a bounded complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces: truncate to the finite interval between the lowest and highest degrees in which cohomology is nonzero, and split the resulting bounded complex into the direct sum of its cohomology spaces placed in their degrees, using that every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits. Both sides are therefore equivalent to the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional vector spaces, with morphisms computed by the injective models of [F2].

On the point inverse and direct image of the identity are exact identity functors, and every section has compact support, so the proper-support functor is also the exact identity. Their derived functors are therefore identities. In the exceptional candidate of [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]], the fibre opens are only the point and the empty set; compact sections are exact, giving dimension bound $d=0$, and the constant sheaf $k$ is itself $c$-soft, so take $K=k[0]$. For a bounded finite-dimensional complex $B$ every term is injective over $k$, and the candidate has sections $\operatorname{Hom}_k^\bullet(k,B)=B$ on the point and zero on the empty set. Thus $f^!$ is the identity with its ordinary evaluation adjunction, and $\omega_{\operatorname{pt}}=a_{\operatorname{pt}}^!k=k[0]$. The ordinary-operations lemma [[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]] identifies tensor and internal Hom with the finite signed complexes: $(A\otimes B)^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}A^p\otimes_kB^q$, with $d(a\otimes b)=d_Aa\otimes b+(-1)^pa\otimes d_Bb$, and $\mathcal Hom^n(A,B)=\prod_p\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^p,B^{p+n})$, with $d\varphi=d_B\varphi-(-1)^n\varphi d_A$. Their terms and amplitudes are finite, so they belong to the category identified in step 1.1. Here $f_*$ and $f_!$ in the Example denote their derived operations, which coincide with their exact underived functors in this case.

Apply [F3] to the constant sheaf $\mathcal F=k_{\mathbb C}$ on $X=\mathbb C$, with $U=\mathbb C^*$ and $Z=\{0\}$: the restriction $k_{\mathbb C}|_{\mathbb C^*}$ is the constant sheaf $k_{\mathbb C^*}$, the restriction to the closed point is $k$, and the sequence reads $0\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to0$, the terms being computed by [F5] for the extension by zero. Stalkwise the middle sheaf is exact: at $x\neq0$ the stalk of $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ is $k$ and the stalk of $i_*k$ is $0$, while at $0$ the first stalk is $0$ and the last is $k$; the quotient of $k_{\mathbb C}$ by $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ has no stalks off $\{0\}$, and by [F4] it is canonically the pushforward $i_*k$ of its restriction to the closed point. All maps are $k$-linear, since they are obtained from the canonical adjunction units of [F5] applied to $k$-sheaves.

View $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k$ as a chain map of complexes concentrated in degree $0$, and let $C$ be its mapping cone with the convention of [F6], so $C^{-1}=k_{\mathbb C}$, $C^0=i_*k$ and the differential $C^{-1}\to C^0$ is the map of step 2.2. Its cohomology is $H^{-1}(C)=\ker(k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k)=j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ by the exactness of step 2.2 and $H^0(C)=\operatorname{coker}(k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k)=0$, so $C$ is quasi-isomorphic to $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$, since the two complexes have the same single nonzero cohomology sheaf in degree $-1$. By the rotation property of cone triangles in [F7], the triangle $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to C\to k_{\mathbb C}[1]$ is isomorphic to the distinguished triangle $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$, the ordinary localization triangle of the open subset $\mathbb C^*$; all three sheaves are constructible for the two-stratum stratification $\{\mathbb C^*,\{0\}\}$ of the line, so the triangle lies in $D_c^b(\mathbb C;k)$ by [F1].
